title: Where, O Death, Are Your Plagues?
summary: Ephraim, once honored among the tribes, has died through Baal worship and keeps making silver idols and kissing calves. The God who knew Israel in the wilderness will now fall on it like a lion, a leopard, and a bear robbed of her cubs, and the kings Israel demanded will not save it. In the middle of the doom God speaks of ransoming his people from Sheol and death, but the chapter ends with Samaria's fall by the sword.
story: This is Hosea's last and darkest word of judgment before the call to return in chapter 14. It gathers the book's themes one more time: idolatry, forgetfulness of the God of the exodus, reliance on kings, and the refusal to be born into new life. The northern kingdom is now pictured as already dead or dying. Yet verse 14 contains words that Paul would later make into a song of resurrection, and that tension between certain death and a God who ransoms from death is the ground on which the book's final chapter stands.
historical:
Verse 1 looks back over Israel's history. The tribe of Ephraim had once been preeminent: Joshua came from it, and Jeroboam I, the first king of the northern kingdom, was an Ephraimite. When Ephraim spoke, others trembled. The turn to Baal probably recalls the reign of Ahab and Jezebel in the ninth century BC, when Baal worship was promoted by the crown (1 Kings 16:31-33), and Hosea treats that apostasy as the moment Ephraim began to die. The calves of verse 2 are the golden calves at Bethel and Dan set up by Jeroboam I, now multiplied in smaller cast images.

The demand for "a king and princes" in verse 10 echoes Israel's original request to Samuel for a king (1 Samuel 8), and may also refer to the rapid turnover of northern kings in Hosea's own day, when one ruler after another was murdered and replaced. God gave kings in anger and took them away in wrath. Verse 16 (numbered 14:1 in the Hebrew Bible) describes the fall of Samaria, which came in 722 BC after a siege of about three years by the Assyrian king Shalmaneser V, with the deportations completed under his successor Sargon II. The atrocities it names were standard in ancient conquest.
cultural:
Hosea's images come from rural life. Morning mist and dew vanish as the sun rises; chaff blows away from a threshing floor when grain is tossed into the wind; smoke escapes through a window opening (houses had no chimneys, only a hole or lattice to let smoke out). All four images describe something without substance or staying power. The lion, leopard, and bear were real predators in ancient Israel's hills and thickets, and a mother bear robbed of her cubs was proverbial for ferocity (2 Samuel 17:8; Proverbs 17:12).

Kissing an idol was an act of homage (compare 1 Kings 19:18, where some refused to kiss Baal). The phrase in verse 2 translated "They offer human sacrifice" is ambiguous in Hebrew; it can also be read as a description of the worshipers themselves: people who offer sacrifices are kissing calves. Either way the point is the absurdity of people bowing to animals of their own making. Sheol, in verse 14, was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, the shadowy place where everyone went at death. Birth imagery in verse 13 relies on the danger of childbirth in the ancient world: a child who does not come out at the right time puts both mother and child at mortal risk.
literary: The chapter swings between retrospect and threat. It opens with Ephraim's past glory and death (verse 1), then moves through a series of short units: idol-making and its emptiness (verses 2 to 3), God's faithfulness since Egypt and Israel's forgetfulness (verses 4 to 6), God as predator (verses 7 to 8), the failure of kings (verses 9 to 11), and the stored-up guilt and failed birth (verses 12 to 13). Verse 14 stands out with its address to Death and Sheol, and the closing verses return to the east wind and the sword. Verses 4 to 6 echo Deuteronomy 8, which warned that when Israel ate and was satisfied its heart would become proud and it would forget the LORD.

outline.t: Ephraim's death through Baal and its passing idols
The God who knew them in the wilderness now falls on them
Stored-up guilt, a failed birth, and the word to Death
The east wind and Samaria's fall

doctrines.note: Verse 4 is one of the Old Testament's strongest statements of exclusive devotion: "you know no God but Me, for there is no Savior besides Me". The one who brought Israel out of Egypt is the only God and the only Savior; everything else Israel trusts is mist and smoke.

The chapter shows idolatry's irony. People take their own silver, hire craftsmen, and then bow down and kiss what they made. Idols have no substance, and those who trust them become like them, as insubstantial as dew and chaff.

Verse 14 speaks of ransom from Sheol and redemption from death, even in a chapter of judgment. Whether it is read as promise or threat in its immediate setting, the Bible's larger story treats God as the one who has power over death itself.

words.note: Yasha, to save or deliver. It appears in verse 4 ("no Savior besides Me") and verse 10 ("Where is your king now to save you"). The contrast is deliberate: Israel wanted kings to save it, but only God can. The name Jesus (Yeshua in Hebrew) is built from this root.

Padah, to ransom. The word describes paying a price to release someone, like the redemption of a firstborn son (Exodus 13:13). In verse 14 God speaks of ransoming his people "from the power of Sheol", taking death itself as the power that holds them.

Ga'al, to redeem, the verb for the act of a kinsman-redeemer who bought back family land or a relative sold into debt, as Boaz did for Ruth. Paired with padah in verse 14, it presents God as the family member who acts to rescue his own from Death.

Sheol, the realm of the dead. It is not the same as the later idea of hell as a place of punishment; in most Old Testament passages it is simply where the dead go. In verse 14 Sheol and Death are addressed as if they were powers or persons, and God calls for their plagues and their sting.

christ: Paul quotes verse 14 at the climax of his great chapter on the resurrection. After describing the dead being raised imperishable, he taunts death with Hosea's questions, following a Greek form of the verse that asks where death's victory and sting are, and then gives thanks to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:54-57). Whatever the verse meant in Hosea's immediate setting (see the hard question), Paul read it as God's final word over death, spoken fully when Christ rose. The chapter also sets up the gospel's claim about who saves. Hosea insists there is no Savior besides the LORD; the New Testament names Jesus as Savior and, in doing so, confesses him as one with the God of Israel.

hard.q: Is verse 14 a promise of rescue or a threat of death?
hard.a: The Hebrew of verse 14 can be read two ways, and translations differ. Many, including the BSB, read the first lines as promises ("I will ransom them from the power of Sheol") and the middle lines as a triumphant taunt of death. Others read the opening as questions (Shall I ransom them from Sheol? Shall I redeem them from Death?) with an implied no, and the middle lines as God summoning Death to bring its plagues against Israel. The final line, "Compassion is hidden from My eyes", and the verses on either side, which are all judgment, support the threatening reading in context. The promising reading draws strength from Hosea's pattern of sudden turns to hope (11:8-9; 14:4) and from Paul's use in 1 Corinthians 15. Some interpreters hold both together: in the short term God will not spare Samaria, but his ultimate purpose is to defeat death itself. Readers can recognize that the immediate sense is disputed while seeing why the church has heard gospel in it.

questions: Hosea says that when Israel was satisfied, its heart became proud and it forgot God. Where does comfort make you forgetful of him?
Israel looked to kings and princes to save it. What do you tend to look to for security that cannot finally save?
How does reading Hosea 13:14 alongside 1 Corinthians 15 shape the way you think about death?
